sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Missouri?
sections.html:
Record it with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits. Section 442.380 says every written instrument that conveys real estate, or affects it in law or equity, goes on record in that county's recorder office once it has been properly acknowledged or proved.

The office name changes from county to county. In Moniteau County, for example, the circuit clerk also acts as recorder, and the combined office is on the courthouse's first floor at 200 E. Main Street in California (the Missouri Association of Counties lists it at 573-796-2071). Other counties keep a separate recorder of deeds. Call the county where your house stands before you mail anything.

A deed does not have to be recorded to bind the two people who signed it. Section 442.400 makes an unrecorded instrument invalid against everyone except the parties and anyone with actual notice of it. In practice that means a buyer who skips recording can lose to a later purchaser or lender who records first without knowing about the earlier deed.

sections.h2: What must a Missouri deed contain before the recorder will accept it?
sections.html:
It needs the grantor's signature, a proper acknowledgment, a legal description, and a mailing address for at least one grantee. Those four items come from three different statutes, so sellers often miss one.

  • Signature. Under section 442.130, the party granting the land signs it, or a lawful agent does.
  • Marital status. The same section requires any written instrument conveying real estate to say whether each individual grantor, mortgagor or other signer is married or unmarried.
  • Acknowledgment. The signature must be acknowledged or proved before a court officer or notary. Inside Missouri that means a court with a seal, a judge, justice or clerk of it, or a notary public (section 442.150). Notaries in other states can take an acknowledgment too.
  • Legal description and grantee address. Section 59.330 requires a legal description of the land, plus a mailing address for one grantee on every deed except easements and rights of way. A recorder may refuse a deed that lacks either, though the statute adds that the deed's validity and its constructive notice are unaffected by the omission.

The acknowledgment certificate has its own wording rules. Section 442.210 sets out sample certificates for individuals, for people signing through an attorney in fact, and for corporations, and the notary adds a signature and title at the end.

sections.h2: How should the pages be formatted for a Missouri recorder?
sections.html:
Format rules are strict enough that a recorder may refuse a deed over margins alone. They are listed in subsection 1 of section 59.310, and a title company usually handles them, but a seller preparing a quitclaim or family deed on their own should check each one.

  • Pages printed on one side only, not permanently bound, with no stapled attachments except what a statute demands.
  • Type no smaller than eight point, in black or dark ink, on white or light paper of at least twenty pound weight.
  • A top margin of at least three inches on the first page, kept clear for the recorder's certification, and at least three quarters of an inch on all other sides.
  • Signatures in dark ink with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped beneath.

The first page, below that three inch margin, must show the document title, its date, every grantor's name and marital status, every grantee's name, any statutory addresses, the legal description, and the book and page of any referenced record. A document that misses the format can still be recorded, but the recorder may add a $25 fee. Some documents are exempt from the format rules altogether: those signed before January 1, 2002, military separation papers, documents executed outside the United States, certified copies, documents where an original party has died or become incapacitated, and court judgments. A rejected document must come back with a written reason.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Missouri?
sections.html:
The base charge is $5 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, for any deed or instrument except plats and surveys. A three page warranty deed therefore costs $11 to record, plus whatever extra the situation triggers.

The recorder may also set a reasonable fee for other use of equipment, staff time and office facilities, and for duplicate records in a medium other than paper. Missouri's recorder fees are statutory, but ask the office for its current total, because a county can add charges that the statute permits.

sections.h2: Can you record a Missouri deed electronically?
sections.html:
Only if your county recorder has chosen to offer it. Section 59.563 lets the recorder of deeds in any county or municipality set up an electronic format for recording and filing, and it also says no recorder has to establish, accept or transmit documents electronically.

That leaves three practical routes for a seller or buyer. A title or escrow company can submit the deed for you at closing. You can deliver the paper original in person to the recorder. Or you can mail it with a check for the page fees and a return address. Whichever way you choose, send the original signed and acknowledged deed, not a photocopy, because the recorder keeps the instrument and returns a stamped copy or the original, depending on the office.

When the deed carries a signer who has died or become incapacitated, such as a deed signed years ago and never filed, the format exemption in section 59.310 applies. Ask the recorder how they want that kind of document presented.

sections.h2: Does recording a deed matter when you sell a house for cash?
sections.html:
Yes, because the buyer's title depends on it. A cash buyer in Missouri still expects the seller's deed to be signed, acknowledged and filed in the right county, and a lender or title insurer will search the recorder's index for competing deeds, liens and old mortgages that were never released.

If your house came to you through a death, the path to a clean title often runs through the recorder. A beneficiary deed must already be on file before the owner died to work, and a small estate affidavit becomes effective evidence of ownership when a copy is filed with the recorder in each county where the real estate sits. Missouri's other deed topics, including transfer on death deeds, build on the same recording rules described above.

Before listing a house, pull your current vesting deed from the recorder and check that the names, marital status statements and legal description match what you plan to sign. A mismatch found at closing can delay the sale by days or weeks.

faqs.q: What is the fee to record a deed in Missouri?
faqs.a: The statutory fee is $5 for the first page and $3 for each page after that, excluding plats and surveys. Missouri adds $25 for a document that fails the format rules. Ask the recorder for the total for your pages.

faqs.q: Does a Missouri deed need to be notarized?
faqs.a: It must be acknowledged or proved and certified, and in Missouri a notary public can take the acknowledgment, as can a court with a seal or its judge, justice or clerk. Section 442.150 lists who may do it inside and outside the state.

faqs.q: Is a deed valid if it is never recorded in Missouri?
faqs.a: It is valid between the two parties and anyone who had actual notice of it, but section 442.400 makes it ineffective against others until it is deposited with the recorder. Record promptly to protect the new owner.

faqs.q: Can a recorder of deeds in Missouri reject my deed?
faqs.a: Yes. A recorder may refuse a document that fails the format rules in section 59.310, or a deed that lacks a legal description or a grantee's mailing address under section 59.330. A rejected document comes back with the reason in writing.

faqs.q: Do I have to say if I am married on a Missouri deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 442.130 requires every written instrument conveying real estate to state whether each individual signing as grantor or mortgagor is married or unmarried. Put it in the body of the deed next to the name.
